title: A shabad for every moment
hook: Sikhs mark birth, marriage and death with particular hymns

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas close, and your line: a whole people prays. Whose name did you say aloud? Today a new part of the path begins: hymns for a whole life. Day six hundred forty-six.

Hum the first song you danced to at a wedding. Now the song that was playing in the car the summer you were seventeen. Now the one they played at your grandfather's funeral. Some songs get welded to moments like that: a private soundtrack. Sikh life has a shared soundtrack like that. The same hymns, sung at the same turning points, by family after family, generation after generation. A child born, a couple married, a life ended: each has its hymns, and some children can hum them before they can read.
screen: `THE SONG FROM THE WEDDING.` → `A PRIVATE SOUNDTRACK.` → `A SHARED ONE, FOR GENERATIONS.`

segments.voice: The word is shabad. It means word, and in Sikh usage it means two things at once. A shabad is a hymn, one composition from the Guru Granth Sahib. And the Shabad is the Word itself, the voice of the Guru, the presence of the One in sound. When a shabad is sung, Sikhs understand both are happening. And the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib are meant to be sung. The scripture is arranged by raag, musical mode, each raag with its own mood and, tradition says, its own time of day. Kirtan, singing those hymns with music, is at the heart of worship. Now look at a life. When a child is born, there are shabads of joy and thanks. When a couple marries, they walk four rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib while the lavan, four verses by Guru Ram Das, are sung. At the end of every day, and at the end of a life, Kirtan Sohila is sung. Guru Nanak even wrote a set of hymns for mourning, the alaahniaan, in Raag Vadhans, on ang 578, which turn the old songs of lament toward the One. For the next five weeks, this part of the path walks through shabads like these: hymns about wealth and greed, longing and friendship, night and morning, birth, marriage and death. Some you may recognize. Some will be new. Each one is a hymn Sikhs reach for at a particular moment of life. The idea isn't to memorize a playlist. It's to have, for every moment, words and a melody that point beyond the moment itself.
screen: `SHABAD: A HYMN, AND THE WORD.` · `ARRANGED BY RAAG, TO BE SUNG.` · `BIRTH, MARRIAGE, NIGHT, DEATH.` · `FIVE WEEKS OF SHABADS FOR A LIFE.` · then, large: `A HYMN FOR EVERY MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one song tied to a memory, any song, sacred or not. Let it play in your head. Notice where it takes you: a room, a face, a season. Notice whether the feeling comes back faster than a photograph would bring it. Kirtan works with that same pull of melody. Then, if you know any shabad, even just its first line or a single Waheguru sung to a tune, let it play next. If you don't, just rest in the silence after your song. The bell holds the time.
Shabad. A hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Word itself. Sikhs sing particular shabads at birth, marriage, the close of each day and the end of a life.
Your line: a hymn for every moment. Today, notice when a song comes into your head on its own, and ask what moment it belongs to. Day six hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib in kirtan, and mark life's turning points with particular hymns: shabads of thanks at a birth, the lavan at a wedding, Kirtan Sohila at night and at a funeral.
